proof-finite-mobius-reconstruction-v2.title: Shared proof: exact reconstruction of every masked output

assumptions.text_md: The coalition is finite. The games and coefficient functions are arbitrary real-valued functions on finite subsets; continuity, differentiability, independence and a zero output baseline are unnecessary.
The ambient universe may be infinite, but every coalition in a sum is finite. Paper applications fix a finite universe and use its powerset.

definitions.text_md: The interaction is a finite alternating sum. Since the summation subset is contained in the target, the cardinality difference in its exponent is a nonnegative integer.
Reconstruction sums all coefficients activated by the retained-variable set.
The insertion difference compares retaining the distinguished variable with masking it. The insertion lemma below is used only when that variable is absent from the target.

proof-finite-mobius-reconstruction-v2.overview: Insertion separates subsets with and without the new variable. The insertion interaction becomes a finite difference; strengthened induction reconstructs both games and cancels the intermediate output.
proof-finite-mobius-reconstruction-v2.completion_scope: The public finite-set reconstruction theorem and its actual library induction; paper specializations are separate.
proof-finite-mobius-reconstruction-v2.example_md: For two variables with mask outputs 2, 5, 7 and 13, the dividends are 2, 3, 5 and 3. Their full sum is 13, the empty-mask sum is 2, and singleton reconstruction gives 5 and 7. If only the full output 13 were required, coefficients 0, 0, 0 and 13 would also fit that one mask but fail all others. Hence the universal mask requirement matters.
caveats: The human proof explains the existing library declarations; its five steps do not introduce five new Lean theorems. The checked scope consists of the library theorem and separately compiled paper adapters.
Every subset sum includes the empty coefficient. If it is omitted, add the output baseline outside the sum.

The source uses double sums and binomial cancellation; the library uses insertion induction or converse inversion. These are separately identified proof routes, not a claim of line-by-line formal translation.

proof_steps.title: Partition the subsets into two families
proof_steps.body_md: Fix finite $S$ and $i\notin S$. Every subset of $S\cup\{i\}$ either excludes $i$, and is a subset $T$ of $S$, or includes $i$, and uniquely equals $T\cup\{i\}$ with $T\subseteq S$. The families are disjoint and exhaustive, so any finite sum of a function $F$ splits into these two sums. The empty subset occurs in the first family; empty $T$ in the second family produces $\{i\}$.
proof_steps.justification: The explicit bijections for subsets with and without the inserted variable.

proof_steps.title: Expand the signs to obtain the insertion difference
proof_steps.body_md: Every $T\subseteq S$ excludes $i$, so the two inserted cardinalities are $|S|+1$ and $|T|+1$. Put $k=|S|-|T|\ge0$. The coefficient of $g(T)$ is $(-1)^{k+1}=-(-1)^k$, and the coefficient of $g(T\cup\{i\})$ is $(-1)^k$. Combining the paired terms gives $(-1)^k[g(T\cup\{i\})-g(T)]$. The resulting sum is the interaction of $\Delta_i g$ on $S$.
proof_steps.justification: Insertion cardinalities, the recurrence for integer powers, and finite distributivity.

proof_steps.title: Strengthen the induction statement and handle the empty set
proof_steps.body_md: Induct by inserting elements into finite $S$, with the strengthened statement that reconstruction holds for every game $g$. This quantification is necessary because the next step applies induction to the new game $\Delta_i g$. When $S=\varnothing$, its only subset is itself; the exponent is zero, so both interaction and reconstruction equal $g(\varnothing)$. No zero-baseline assumption is used.
proof_steps.justification: Finite-set insertion induction and the exact empty-interaction formula.

proof_steps.title: Apply induction to each of the two sums
proof_steps.body_md: Assume that every game $h$ is reconstructed on $S$, and let $i\notin S$. Split the reconstruction on $S\cup\{i\}$ into the two families from the first step. In the family containing $i$, each $T\subseteq S$ still excludes $i$, so apply the insertion-difference identity term by term. The two sums become reconstruction for $g$ and reconstruction for $\Delta_i g$ on $S$. The same strengthened induction hypothesis gives $g(S)$ and $\Delta_i g(S)$ respectively.
proof_steps.justification: Subset partition, the insertion identity, and induction quantified over all games.

proof_steps.title: Cancel the intermediate output and finish induction
proof_steps.body_md: By definition, $\Delta_i g(S)=g(S\cup\{i\})-g(S)$. Adding it to $g(S)$ cancels the intermediate value and leaves the required output on the inserted set. The empty case and insertion step cover every finite set. For a paper application, instantiate the game with $g(S)=v(x_S)$ using one fixed model, input and mask rule.
proof_steps.justification: The finite-difference definition and real addition and subtraction.

proof-finite-mobius-uniqueness-v2.title: Shared proof: uniqueness of coefficients reconstructing all masks

assumptions.text_md: The coalition is finite. The games and coefficient functions are arbitrary real-valued functions on finite subsets; continuity, differentiability, independence and a zero output baseline are unnecessary.
The ambient universe may be infinite, but every coalition in a sum is finite. Paper applications fix a finite universe and use its powerset.
The same coefficients must reconstruct every finite subset in the domain, including the empty set. Reconstruction at one specified coalition is insufficient.

proof-finite-mobius-uniqueness-v2.overview: Prove converse Möbius inversion for arbitrary coefficients, then substitute the reconstruction equality at every mask and conclude pointwise equality.
proof-finite-mobius-uniqueness-v2.completion_scope: Coefficient uniqueness and the converse inversion actually used by the library; finite-universe paper quantifiers are recorded by separate adapters.
proof-finite-mobius-uniqueness-v2.example_md: For two variables with mask outputs 2, 5, 7 and 13, the dividends are 2, 3, 5 and 3. Their full sum is 13, the empty-mask sum is 2, and singleton reconstruction gives 5 and 7. If only the full output 13 were required, coefficients 0, 0, 0 and 13 would also fit that one mask but fail all others. Hence the universal mask requirement matters.
caveats: Uniqueness concerns coefficients for one fixed game and the same AND activation rule. It does not assert uniqueness of every explanation framework, causal model or AND–OR decomposition.
The source inducts on cardinality; the library proves converse inversion. This text fully explains the route actually used by the library.
Every subset, including the empty one, must be reconstructed exactly. Fitting only the full input, or fitting approximately, does not satisfy the theorem.

proof_steps.title: Prove converse inversion at the empty set
proof_steps.body_md: First prove $I_{R_d}(S)=d(S)$ for an arbitrary coefficient function $d$, without using the reconstruction hypothesis. Induct on finite $S$ and keep $d$ universally quantified. At the empty set, $R_d(\varnothing)=d(\varnothing)$, and the empty interaction of this game has that same value. Thus the empty coefficient is fixed rather than an additional free parameter.
proof_steps.justification: The definitions and strengthened finite-set induction.

proof_steps.title: The difference of a reconstruction is another reconstruction
proof_steps.body_md: For $i\notin S$, define $e(U)=d(U\cup\{i\})$. Every $T\subseteq S$ excludes $i$, so splitting the subsets of $T\cup\{i\}$ gives $R_d(T\cup\{i\})=R_d(T)+\sum_{U\subseteq T}d(U\cup\{i\})$. Subtraction leaves $R_e(T)$. This identity is used only for $T\subseteq S$: when $i\in T$, the two-family argument would no longer be disjoint.
proof_steps.justification: The subset partition, cancellation of finite sums, and the definition of the new coefficient function.

proof_steps.title: Use local equality to prove the insertion step
proof_steps.body_md: The insertion lemma gives $I_{R_d}(S\cup\{i\})=I_{\Delta_i R_d}(S)$. The interaction on $S$ reads only values at subsets of $S$, where the previous step proves that $\Delta_i R_d$ equals $R_e$. Hence its interaction equals $I_{R_e}(S)$. Apply the induction hypothesis for the arbitrary function $e$ to obtain $e(S)=d(S\cup\{i\})$. This proves converse inversion on the inserted set.
proof_steps.justification: Insertion differences, congruence on the subsets actually used, and strengthened induction.

proof_steps.title: Substitute the reconstruction hypothesis for every mask
proof_steps.body_md: Restore the assumption that the same $d$ satisfies $R_d(T)=g(T)$ at every finite $T$. For arbitrary $S$, converse inversion gives $d(S)=I_{R_d}(S)$. In this finite sum every argument $U$ is a subset of $S$, so the assumption replaces $R_d(U)$ by $g(U)$ term by term. The resulting sum is $I_g(S)$. Coefficients are not chosen afresh for each mask.
proof_steps.justification: Converse inversion and the reconstruction equality at each subset.

proof_steps.title: Conclude function equality and check the application domain
proof_steps.body_md: Since $S$ is arbitrary, equality at every finite input gives $d=I_g$. The public result quantifies over all finite subsets of a universe that may itself be infinite; a paper application restricts this universe to its finite $N$. In particular, the empty mask forces $d(\varnothing)=g(\varnothing)$, and a singleton forces $d(\{i\})=g(\{i\})-g(\varnothing)$. Higher coefficients are then fixed by the already determined proper-subset coefficients.
proof_steps.justification: Function extensionality and the finite-universe paper specialization.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Apply the premise at the actual summation argument
proof_steps.body_md: Assume $g_v(U)=g_t(U)+g_u(U)$ for every $U\subseteq N$. For a fixed $A$, each $U\subseteq A$ lies in that domain. The original proof wrote the fixed output at $x_A$ inside the alternating sum; the repaired proof uses the output at the summation argument $x_U$ in every term, preserving the original proposition.

proof_steps.title: Distribute within the finite sum
proof_steps.body_md: For each $U\subseteq A$, distribute its alternating coefficient over the two outputs. Then distribute the finite sum over addition. The two resulting sums are exactly $I_{g_t}(A)$ and $I_{g_u}(A)$.

proof_steps.title: Check the empty set and a constant example
proof_steps.body_md: For $A=\varnothing$, the identity states $b_v=b_t+b_u$; none of these baselines needs to vanish. For constant models with values 2 and 5, their sum has value 7: its empty dividend is 7 and every nonempty dividend is zero.

shared-harsanyi-symmetry.title: Shared proof: symmetry of interactions
assumptions: $S\subseteq N$, $i,j\in N\setminus S$; for every $U\subseteq S$, $g(U\cup\{i\})=g(U\cup\{j\})$.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Pair subsets that include or exclude the distinguished variable
proof_steps.body_md: Since $i,j\notin S$, every subset of $S\cup\{i\}$ uniquely has the form $U$ or $U\cup\{i\}$ for $U\subseteq S$. Insertion increases cardinality by one, giving opposite signs. Each $U$ excludes both distinguished variables, so the equal-cooperation premise applies to every paired term.

proof_steps.title: Replace equal cooperation outputs term by term
proof_steps.body_md: Replace $g(U\cup\{i\})$ by $g(U\cup\{j\})$ using the premise; leave $g(U)$ unchanged. Recombine the terms with and without $j$ to obtain the interaction on $S\cup\{j\}$. Equality also holds when $i=j$, so no distinctness hypothesis is added.

proof_steps.title: Check the empty environment
proof_steps.body_md: When $S=\varnothing$, equal singleton outputs have the same subtraction of the common baseline. For baseline 7, singleton outputs 8 and 8, and two-variable output 12, both singleton dividends are 1; if the two variables are distinct, the pair dividend is 3.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Define the relabeled game and the subset bijection
proof_steps.body_md: For a permutation $\pi$, define $g^\pi(V)=g(\pi^{-1}V)$. The map $U\mapsto\pi U$ bijects the subsets of $S$ with those of $\pi S$ and preserves cardinality. Its inverse sends $V$ to $\pi^{-1}V$.

proof_steps.title: Reindex the finite sum by this bijection
proof_steps.body_md: Corresponding terms have exponent $|\pi S|-|\pi U|=|S|-|U|$ and output $g^\pi(\pi U)=g(U)$. Therefore every summand agrees and the sums agree.

proof_steps.title: Check a swap and the baseline
proof_steps.body_md: For two variables with outputs 7, 8, 9 and 13 at the empty, first singleton, second singleton and full masks, the dividends are 7, 1, 2 and 3. Swapping the variable names swaps the singleton dividends while leaving the empty and pair dividends unchanged. A permutation fixes the empty set, so it also preserves the output baseline.

shared-harsanyi-recursive.title: Shared proof: context difference for inserting a variable

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Define the context in which the variable is always present
proof_steps.body_md: Define $g_i(U)=g(U\cup\{i\})$. The original interaction conditioned on the presence of $i$ is $I_{g_i}(S)$. The empty value of this conditional game is $g(\{i\})$, which need not equal the original baseline $g(\varnothing)$.

proof_steps.title: Pair the subsets and check their signs
proof_steps.body_md: With $i\notin S$, the subset $U\cup\{i\}$ has exponent $|S|+1-(|U|+1)=|S|-|U|$. The term for $U$ has one extra minus sign. Pairing the families gives the game $g_i(U)-g(U)$; linearity separates its two interactions.

proof_steps.title: Check the empty case and a numerical difference
proof_steps.body_md: For mask outputs 7, 8, 9 and 13 on two variables, the dividends are 7, 1, 2 and 3. With $S=\{2\}$ and $i=1$, the conditional interaction is $13-8=5$, the original one is $9-7=2$, and their difference is the pair dividend 3. For an empty environment, the formula yields the singleton output minus the baseline, without asserting that it vanishes.

shared-harsanyi-interaction-distribution.title: Shared proof: the unique dividend of a pure AND game
assumptions: $T,S\subseteq N$, $c\in\mathbb R$; $u_T(U)=c\mathbf1_{T\subseteq U}$. Empty $T$ and incomparable sets are included.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Handle every case in which the target is not contained
proof_steps.body_md: If $T\not\subseteq S$, no subset $U$ of $S$ can contain $T$. Thus every output and summand is zero. This includes both proper-subset and incomparable cases; the original proof omitted the latter.

proof_steps.title: Evaluate at the target itself
proof_steps.body_md: If $S=T$, only the subset $U=T$ contributes the output $c$, with coefficient 1; every proper subset contributes zero. This also covers the empty target, whose only summand is the empty-set output $c$.

proof_steps.title: Cancel on strict supersets
proof_steps.body_md: For $T\subsetneq S$, the potentially nonzero subsets uniquely equal $T\cup B$, with $B\subseteq S\setminus T$. Their exponents are $|S\setminus T|-|B|$. Choose an element of the nonempty difference, and pair each $B$ excluding it with the subset including it. The two signs are opposite, so the whole sum vanishes.

proof_steps.title: Check the empty target and an incomparable set
proof_steps.body_md: An empty target gives the constant game $c$, with only its empty dividend nonzero. With $N=\{1,2\}$, $T=\{1\}$ and $c=3$, the four outputs are 0, 3, 0 and 3, and the dividends are 0, 3, 0 and 0. The incomparable set $\{2\}$ is covered by the first case.

shared-harsanyi-marginal-decomposition.title: Shared proof: dividend decomposition of a higher marginal

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Reconstruct every output used by the difference
proof_steps.body_md: Fix disjoint $T$ and $S$. For each $L\subseteq T$, reconstruct $g(L\cup S)$. Every subset $K$ of this union uniquely decomposes into $A\cup U$, where $A=K\cap L\subseteq L$ and $U=K\cap S\subseteq S$. Disjointness prevents duplicate representations.

proof_steps.title: Exchange finite sums and cancel within each environment subset
proof_steps.body_md: Group first by $U$, then by $A\subseteq T$. Every $L$ containing $A$ uniquely equals $A\cup B$, with $B\subseteq T\setminus A$. If $A\ne T$, pairing subsets of the nonempty difference cancels opposite signs. If $A=T$, only empty $B$ remains with coefficient 1. Therefore each $U$ contributes exactly $w_{T\cup U}$.

proof_steps.title: Check both empty-set boundaries
proof_steps.body_md: For the two-variable outputs 7, 8, 9 and 13, the difference for $T=\{1\}$ and $S=\{2\}$ is $13-9=4$, and its dividend sum is $1+3=4$. When $T$ is empty, the identity is reconstruction of $g(S)$; when $S$ is empty, both sides equal $w_T$.

shared-harsanyi-factorial-convolution.title: Shared auxiliary proof: finite factorial convolution, including empty boundaries

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Prove the finite factorial convolution
proof_steps.body_md: For finite $R$ of size $m$, define $F_R(a,b)=\sum_{A\subseteq R}(a+|A|)!(b+m-|A|)!$. Induct on $R$ with the statement strengthened to every nonnegative $a,b$. At the empty set both sides are $a!b!$. Inserting a new element splits the sum as $F_R(a,b+1)+F_R(a+1,b)$. The induction expressions share denominator $(a+b+2)!$ and large factorial $(a+b+m+2)!$. The smaller factorials combine as $a!(b+1)!+(a+1)!b!=a!b!(a+b+2)$. Cancelling this positive factor proves the formula on the inserted set. Every factorial denominator is positive; zero values of $a,b,m$ are included.

proof_steps.title: Sum weights over all supersets of a fixed subset
proof_steps.body_md: Let $k>0$, $L\subseteq E$, $m=|E|$, $l=|L|$ and $R=E\setminus L$. Each $S$ with $L\subseteq S\subseteq E$ uniquely equals $L\cup A$ with $A\subseteq R$. Thus $|S|=l+|A|$ and $|R|=m-l$. Apply the preceding convolution with $a=l$ and $b=k-1$. Use $k(k-1)!=k!$ and cancel the positive large factorial $(m+k)!$ to obtain the displayed weight sum. Both $L=\varnothing$ and $L=E$ are included.

proof_steps.title: Exchange the sums to obtain the weighted finite-difference transform
proof_steps.body_md: Disjointness of $T,E$ gives $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{U\subseteq S}w_{T\cup U}$. Every pair $U\subseteq S\subseteq E$ occurs exactly once, so exchange the finite sums. For fixed $U$, the preceding superset-weight identity supplies precisely the displayed coefficient of $w_{T\cup U}$.

shared-harsanyi-shapley-dividend.title: Shared proof: classical Shapley equals equal dividend allocation
assumptions: $i\in N$; $\phi_g$ is defined by the classical factorial-weighted marginal formula; $n=|N|\ge1$.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Start from the classical factorial-weighted definition
proof_steps.body_md: Let $i\in N$, so $n=|N|\ge1$. Classical Shapley weights each environment marginal $g(S\cup\{i\})-g(S)=\Delta_{\{i\}}g(S)$ by $|S|!(n-|S|-1)!/n!$, for $S\subseteq N\setminus\{i\}$.

proof_steps.title: Prove the finite factorial convolution
Sum weights over all supersets of a fixed subset
Exchange the sums to obtain the weighted finite-difference transform
Check all parameters of the shared identity
proof_steps.body_md: Set $T=\{i\}$, $E=N\setminus\{i\}$ and $k=1$. Then $m=n-1$, and the left weight is exactly the classical Shapley weight. The right coefficient is $\binom{|U|+1}{1}^{-1}=1/(|U|+1)$. The difference target and environment are disjoint and the order is positive, so every premise of the shared identity is satisfied.

proof_steps.title: Check the baseline and a two-variable example
proof_steps.body_md: For outputs 7, 8, 9 and 13, the dividends are 7, 1, 2 and 3. The two Shapley values are $1+3/2=5/2$ and $2+3/2=7/2$, summing to $6=g(N)-b$. The environment may be empty, but a dividend allocated to $i$ always contains $i$ and is nonempty. The baseline is not allocated. For a one-player game the sole environment is empty and its value is the singleton output minus the baseline.

shared-harsanyi-shapley-interaction-divi.title: Shared proof: exact dividend weights for the Shapley interaction index
assumptions: $T\subseteq N$; use the original factorial-weighted SII definition with environment $N\setminus T$, including the empty target.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Keep the original factorial definition and external environment
proof_steps.body_md: Put $t=|T|$, $E=N\setminus T$ and $m=n-t$. SII uses the whole-target finite difference with weight $|S|!(m-|S|)!/(m+1)!$. It does not allocate separately to the members of $T$. The source domain includes both $T=\varnothing$ and $T=N$.

proof_steps.title: Prove the finite factorial convolution
Sum weights over all supersets of a fixed subset
Exchange the sums to obtain the weighted finite-difference transform
Specialize the shared weighted identity to order one
proof_steps.body_md: The target $T$ and its external environment $E$ are disjoint. At $k=1$, each left weight agrees with the original SII definition and each right weight is $1/(|U|+1)$. For $T=N$, the environment is empty and the result is $w_N$. For an empty target, the left side is the indicated weighted average of raw outputs and the right side includes the empty dividend $b$.

proof_steps.title: Check the two-variable boundaries
proof_steps.body_md: For outputs 7, 8, 9 and 13, the dividends are 7, 1, 2 and 3. SII at the full target equals 3; at the first singleton it equals $5/2$. For the empty target the factorial formula gives $7/3+8/6+9/6+13/3=19/2$, agreeing with $7+1/2+2/2+3/3=19/2$ from the dividend formula.

shared-harsanyi-shapley-taylor-dividend.title: Shared proof: all three branches of the Shapley–Taylor index
assumptions: $T\subseteq N$; the original three-branch STI definition at a positive integer order $k>0$. The source does not explicitly state $k>0$; this is the positive-order domain interpretation. Order zero is outside the present verification scope.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: Handle the lower and higher order branches
proof_steps.body_md: At a positive order $k$, if $|T|<k$, the finite difference in the empty environment is $w_T$ by definition; for an empty target its value is $b$. If $|T|>k$, the definition gives zero. These branches require neither division by $n$ nor $n\ge k$.

proof_steps.title: Convert the top-order weight to the shared factorial weight
proof_steps.body_md: If $|T|=k$, positivity and $T\subseteq N$ give $n\ge k\ge1$, so division by $n$ is valid. Put $E=N\setminus T$ and $m=n-k$. For $S\subseteq E$, its size $s$ satisfies $s\le m\le n-1$, making the relevant binomial coefficient positive. Expand its factorial definition and use $k(k-1)!=k!$ to obtain the displayed shared weight.

proof_steps.title: Prove the finite factorial convolution
Sum weights over all supersets of a fixed subset
Exchange the sums to obtain the weighted finite-difference transform
Apply the shared identity at the top order
proof_steps.body_md: The target and environment are disjoint and $k>0$, so the weighted finite-difference identity yields coefficient $\binom{|U|+k}{k}^{-1}$. Combining this with the lower and higher order definition branches proves the full three-branch statement.

proof_steps.title: Check empty targets and two positive orders
proof_steps.body_md: For the outputs 7, 8, 9 and 13, the dividends are 7, 1, 2 and 3. At $k=1$, the empty target has value 7, the singletons have values $5/2$ and $7/2$, and the pair is above the order and has value zero. At $k=2$, the four values are 7, 1, 2 and 3, summing to 13. If the universe is empty and $k\ge1$, only the lower-order empty target remains with value $b$. Positive order is the stated scope interpretation; the source does not explicitly print the inequality.

shared-harsanyi-dummy-nonempty.title: Shared valid property: additive dummy interactions vanish in nonempty environments
assumptions: $i\in N\setminus S$; $S\ne\varnothing$; $c\in\mathbb R$; for every $U\subseteq S$, $g(U\cup\{i\})=g(U)+c$.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend.

proof_steps.title: State the exact domain of the valid public property
proof_steps.body_md: This public result requires $S\ne\varnothing$ and has different quantifiers from the false CVPR proposition; it cannot replace that proposition. Since $i\notin S$ and the marginal is the constant $c$, the interaction containing $i$ equals the interaction of the constant game $c$ on $S$.
proof_steps.justification: The original Sparse statement can use this result if it already excludes empty environments; the original CVPR statement cannot.

proof_steps.title: Cancel all subsets by an explicit pairing
proof_steps.body_md: Pair subsets with and without $i$ to obtain $I_g(S\cup\{i\})=c\sum_{U\subseteq S}(-1)^{|S|-|U|}$. Choose $j\in S$, possible because $S$ is nonempty, and pair subsets with and without $j$. Their signs cancel, giving zero. For empty $S$, the sum equals $c$, demonstrating why the boundary condition is necessary.
proof_steps.justification: No assumption $g(\varnothing)=0$ is needed; the premises imply $c=g(\{i\})-g(\varnothing)$.

shared-harsanyi-or-reconstruction.title: Shared proof: exact reconstruction by the OR complement transform
assumptions: $T\subseteq N$; $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$. Nonempty OR dividends are the negative AND transform of the complement game; the empty OR dividend is the original output baseline.

definitions.body_md: Fix a finite universe $N$. A game $g:\mathcal P(N)\to\mathbb R$ has output baseline $b=g(\varnothing)$ and interaction $I_g(A)=\sum_{U\subseteq A}(-1)^{|A|-|U|}g(U)$. Write $w_A=I_g(A)$. Every subset sum includes the empty set, and $w_\varnothing=b$. The finite difference is $\Delta_Tg(S)=\sum_{L\subseteq T}(-1)^{|T|-|L|}g(L\cup S)$. No zero output baseline is assumed. Centering $g_0=g-b$ removes only the empty dividend. For nonempty targets, $O_g^N(S)=-I_{g^c}(S)$ where $g^c(L)=g(N\setminus L)$; the empty OR coefficient is $g(\varnothing)$.

proof_steps.title: Intersecting subsets are a difference of two powersets
proof_steps.body_md: For $T\subseteq N$ and $S\subseteq N$, disjointness from $T$ is equivalent to $S\subseteq N\setminus T$. Therefore the intersecting family is $\mathcal P(N)\setminus\mathcal P(N\setminus T)$. The second powerset is contained in the first, so its sum is subtracted from the full sum. The empty set belongs to both full families and to neither intersecting family.

proof_steps.title: Reconstruct the negative complement game twice
proof_steps.body_md: Let $f(L)=-h(N\setminus L)$. Linearity shows that each nonempty OR coefficient equals $I_f(S)$. Every intersecting set is nonempty, so substitute these coefficients throughout the intersecting sum. Apply reconstruction on $N$ and on $N\setminus T$ to obtain $f(N)-f(N\setminus T)=-h(\varnothing)+h(T)$. The final complement equality uses the checked premise $T\subseteq N$.

proof_steps.title: Add back the separately defined empty OR baseline
proof_steps.body_md: The empty OR coefficient is $h(\varnothing)=v_{or}(x_\varnothing)$. Adding it to the intersecting sum gives $v_{or}(x_T)$. For empty $T$, the intersecting family is empty and only the baseline remains; for $T=N$, the full output is recovered. This also avoids double-counting source cases when $T$ is empty.
